title: Why git got slow, and what gc actually does
summary: Loose objects pile up, refs multiply, and everyday commands crawl. Watch garbage collection pack thousands of objects into one file, and see exactly which of your commits it would delete.
mental_model: Every write creates a loose object — one small file. gc bundles them into a packfile with delta compression, packs the refs into one file, and deletes unreachable objects older than the expiry. Fewer, bigger files means faster everything.

steps.title: Generate a lot of loose objects
steps.why: Thirty commits, each writing a commit, a tree and a blob. In a real repository this is a fortnight of work — and every one of those objects is a separate file on disk.

actions.run: sh -c 'for i in $(seq 1 30); do printf "print(%d)\n" $i > app.py; git add app.py; git commit -q -m "Change $i"; done'

steps.title: Add branches that are going away
steps.why: Branch tips keep commits reachable. Deleting the branches makes those commits unreachable — the population gc is designed to consider deleting.

actions.run: sh -c 'for name in alpha beta gamma; do git switch -q -c experiment/$name; printf "experiment %s\n" $name > exp.py; git add exp.py; git commit -q -m "Experiment $name"; git switch -q main; done'

steps.expect: Four branches, each a separate small file under .git/refs/heads.

steps.title: Delete them and see what becomes unreachable
steps.why: The commits still exist and are still reachable through the reflog. `--no-reflogs` asks the harder question: what would be unreachable if the reflog expired?

steps.title: Run garbage collection
steps.why: gc packs the loose objects into a packfile, packs the refs into `.git/packed-refs`, and prunes unreachable objects older than the expiry — two weeks by default, which is why nothing disappears here.
steps.expect: Loose count near zero, one packfile, and refs moved into packed-refs.

steps.title: The experiments survived
steps.why: gc's default prune expiry protects anything younger than two weeks, precisely so a mistaken branch deletion stays recoverable. This is why `gc` is safe to run and `gc --prune=now` is not.
steps.expect: The experiment commits are still there.

steps.title: Now prune for real
steps.why: `--prune=now` ignores the expiry and deletes every unreachable object immediately. This is the command that makes the reflog rescue impossible — run it only when you are certain, such as after purging a secret.
steps.expect: Zero unreachable objects — the experiments are genuinely gone.

steps.title: Schedule maintenance instead of remembering
steps.why: `git maintenance` runs the same work incrementally in the background — packing, prefetching, rewriting the commit-graph. On a large repository the commit-graph alone makes `git log --graph` dramatically faster.

verify.label: a commit-graph was written for faster history traversal
every reachable commit survived — gc never touches reachable history
a commit-graph exists for faster traversal

pitfalls: `git gc` is safe: it only deletes unreachable objects older than two weeks. `git gc --prune=now` is not, and it is what makes reflog recovery impossible.
gc runs automatically when loose objects pass a threshold. If a background gc is what deleted something, `gc.auto 0` stops it while you recover.
Packing does not shrink a repository whose size comes from a large reachable blob. That needs a history rewrite.
`git maintenance register` schedules background upkeep. On big repositories it, plus the commit-graph, is the single biggest speed win available.
A repository with tens of thousands of refs is slow regardless of packing. Prune stale branches and tags too.
cheatsheet: pack objects and refs, prune old unreachable objects
delete unreachable objects immediately — no undo
schedule the upkeep in the background
